title: Ja'far al-Sadiq's school
hookLine: the Ja'fari school, followed by Twelver Shia, is named for the sixth Imam
carry: the school of the sixth imam

lines: A PILGRIMAGE REPORT IN SAHIH MUSLIM.
ONE MAN, HONORED ON BOTH SIDES.
cards: Sahih Muslim holds a long report of the Prophet's pilgrimage, told step by step, from setting out to the standing at Arafat.
Look at who passed it on: Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from the Companion Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. Sunni hadith scholars carried that report through him, and call him al-Sadiq, the truthful.
For Twelver Shia Muslims he is also Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, the sixth Imam. One man, honored on both sides. Today, the school of law that carries his name.

teach.h: THE SCHOOL OF THE TWELVER SHIA.
teach.b: You met him on day 894, beside his father. The Ja'fari school is the school of law followed by Twelver Shia Muslims.
Twelvers recognize a line of Imams from the Prophet's family, beginning with 'Ali, and Ja'far is the sixth. He lived and taught in Medina, after his father, Muhammad al-Baqir.

Shia tradition holds that the Imams carry the Prophet's knowledge, passed from one to the next, and that Ja'far taught openly, on law, on the Qur'an, on belief, which is why the school bears his name.
Sunni Muslims honor him too, as a scholar of the Prophet's household. Reports say Abu Hanifa and Malik sat with him or learned from him; scholars weigh those reports differently.
From inside, its sources are the Qur'an and the sunnah. For Twelvers, the sunnah includes the teachings of the Imams, received through Shia collections such as al-Kafi, gathered by al-Kulayni.
It uses reason, 'aql, which this block met a few weeks ago. And its jurists don't use analogy, qiyas, the way the Sunni schools do; in Shia reports, Ja'far himself warns against it.
One saying attributed to him in al-Kafi, paraphrased: don't judge a man by how long he bows and prostrates; that may be a habit he'd feel lost without.
Look instead at his truthfulness when he speaks, and at how he returns what was entrusted to him. Two plain things: the word you give, and the thing you were trusted with.

how: Twelver Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school of law, which draws on the Qur'an, the sunnah of the Prophet and the teachings of the Imams, and Sunni scholars also honor Ja'far al-Sadiq as a scholar of the Prophet's household.

games.q: you want to know whether to trust someone. the saying in al-Kafi gives you a test. what do you look at?

their truthful speech, and how they return a trust.
games.why: truthful speech and a trust returned. long bowing, the saying warns, may only be a habit.

practice: Say his saying in your own words: don't judge by the length of the bowing; look at truthful speech and a trust returned.
Think of someone you trust and what earned it, then turn it around gently: is there a word you gave, or something you were lent, that's still waiting?
Don't fix it yet; just see it and breathe, and if you pray, you can ask to be trustworthy.
